lead: An Arduino sketch is a C++ program with two required functions. setup() runs once at power-on; loop() repeats forever. Typed variables hold pin numbers and readings. pinMode() selects input or output. digitalWrite() drives a pin HIGH or LOW. digitalRead() samples a digital pin. delay() waits in milliseconds. if/else chooses a branch; Serial.print shows values in the IDE. Only a few universities teach this as a separate programming chapter. Makers use it for buttons, LEDs and relays, such as a doorbell LED that follows a switch.

blocks.text: A sketch is a C++ program. The Arduino core supplies main(), which calls setup() once and then loop() forever. You do not write main(). setup() runs once after reset. loop() repeats forever. Every variable has a type. int stores a whole number, such as pin 13. On AVR boards such as the Uno, int is 16 bits, so it holds -32768 to 32767; use long or unsigned long for larger values. float stores a decimal, such as 2.5. boolean stores true or false. Use const int LED = 13; for a pin that never changes; const blocks accidental writes. Names are case-sensitive. End statements with a semicolon. Comments use // or /* */. Serial.begin(9600); starts serial output at 9600 bits per second. Serial.println(value); prints value and a newline in the Serial Monitor. That is the main debugging tool when no display is attached. A variable declared inside loop() is recreated each pass; a global keeps its value. Use meaningful names: buttonPin, ledPin. The board stores the sketch in flash; variables live in RAM. Choose the smallest type that fits.

sections.h3: Digital I/O functions and control flow

blocks.text: pinMode(pin, mode) sets a pin. mode is INPUT or OUTPUT. OUTPUT can source or sink limited current; use a series resistor for an LED. digitalWrite(pin, value) sets an output pin to HIGH (5 V on most Uno-class boards) or LOW (0 V). digitalRead(pin) returns HIGH or LOW from an input pin; it does not set the pin. delay(ms) blocks for ms milliseconds. if (condition) { } else { } chooses a branch. Use == to compare, not =. Example: read pin 2; if HIGH, set pin 13 HIGH; else LOW. With a pull-down resistor, a released button reads LOW; a pressed button connects 5 V and reads HIGH. The loop repeats this test, so the LED follows the button. delay() stops all other work. Call pinMode(pin, INPUT) or pinMode(pin, INPUT_PULLUP) to state the direction, and give the pin a defined level with a pull resistor. An unconnected input floats and gives random values. A short delay can debounce a noisy button. Check wiring before power.

figure.caption: Pressing the button joins pin 2 to 5 V, so it reads HIGH while 0.5 mA flows through the 10 kΩ pull-down; released, the resistor holds pin 2 at 0 V. The loop reads pin 2 and copies it to the LED on pin 13.

spec.aria: Left, a circuit: 5 volts through a push button to pin 2, with a 10 kilo-ohm resistor from pin 2 to ground carrying 0.5 mA. Right, a flow: setup once, then loop reads pin 2; if HIGH the LED on pin 13 is on, otherwise off, and the loop repeats.

examples.question: A push button connects 5 V to Arduino pin 2. A 10 kΩ resistor pulls pin 2 to ground. An LED is on pin 13. Write setup() and loop() so the LED is on only while the button is pressed. Find the pull-down current when pressed.
steps: 1. Set directions in setup(): pinMode(2, INPUT); pinMode(13, OUTPUT).
2. In loop(), if digitalRead(2) == HIGH, digitalWrite(13, HIGH); else, digitalWrite(13, LOW).
3. Pressed: pin 2 is at 5 V. Pull-down current I = V ÷ R = 5 V ÷ 10 kΩ = 5 ÷ 10000 A = 0.0005 A = 0.5 mA.
4. Released: no 5 V path; the resistor holds pin 2 at 0 V; current is 0 mA.
examples.answer: The sketch lights the LED only while pressed; pull-down current is 0.5 mA when pressed. Any printed 'LED ON' comes from a PC simulation, not from the board.
examples.check:
V = 5.0
R = 10_000.0
I_A = V / R
I_mA = I_A * 1000
print(I_mA)
examples.output: Simulated on a PC: LED ON. The board itself prints nothing.

traps: digitalRead(pin) reads a pin; pinMode(pin, INPUT) sets its direction.
== compares; = assigns. if (x = HIGH) is wrong.
INPUT_PULLUP inverts logic: a button to ground reads LOW when pressed.
delay(1000) is 1000 ms = 1 s, not 1 ms.
A pin set OUTPUT must not be driven by an external voltage source.

quiz.q: Which two functions must every Arduino sketch define?
Why use const int for a pin number?
quiz.a: It marks the pin as fixed, blocks accidental writes, and documents the wiring.

quiz.q: pinMode(7, OUTPUT); digitalWrite(7, HIGH); What voltage appears on pin 7 on a 5 V board?
quiz.a: About 5 V (the supply rail on a 5 V board), provided the load draws less than the pin's safe current, roughly 20 mA for one pin on an Uno-class board.

quiz.q: A button to ground uses INPUT_PULLUP. What does digitalRead return when pressed, and why?
quiz.a: LOW. The internal pull-up holds the pin HIGH when open; pressing connects the pin to ground.

quiz.q: delay(250) follows digitalWrite(13, HIGH). How long is the LED on before the next change?
A sketch reads pin 4 but never calls pinMode(4, INPUT). Why may the reading be unreliable?
quiz.a: The pin is high-impedance and floats, so noise gives random HIGH or LOW values. pinMode(4, INPUT) alone does not help. Use pinMode(4, INPUT_PULLUP) with a button to ground, or fit an external pull-up/pull-down resistor, or drive the pin from a low-impedance source.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, Arduino sketches are often generated from graphical tools or replaced by ESP-IDF and Zephyr. Arduino C++ also supports classes and libraries; reading a library header teaches pin abstraction. Search for “Arduino core” and “avr-libc” to see the code behind pinMode.
